FoveaWAM: Role-Aware 4D World–Action Modeling for Dynamic Manipulation

Abstract

To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target’s pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world–action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target’s past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10× faster than video world–action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks.

Method

Only the target’s pose needs millimeter precision. FoveaWAM represents each part of the scene according to its role:

Target
A metric SE(3) trajectory, read from a short pose history and predicted 400 ms ahead.
Surroundings
Coarse sparse 3D flow, enough to capture the clearance they leave and the motion they impart.
Static scene
Taken from the current RGB-D frame.

OnTimeBench

Existing simulators pause the world while the policy computes. In OnTimeBench the scene keeps moving, so every policy is scored at its own measured latency.

14 tasks in five families

Results

FoveaWAM has the highest success rate at native latency, with 150 ms added, and with the world paused.
